content: Lymphangitis is defined as an inflammation of the lymphatic channels. It is a condition that has been recognized since ancient times, although its precise origins remain unclear. There is no established classification system for lymphangitis. However, based on its etiology, it can be broadly categorized into infectious and non-infectious causes. The underlying cause of lymphangitis varies depending on its clinical presentation. The lymphatic system, which is affected in lymphangitis, is a network of small vessels that are part of the immune system. These vessels transport lymphatic fluid, which is filtered through lymph nodes and the spleen, drained into the subclavian veins via the thoracic duct, and ultimately returned to the circulatory system. The differential diagnosis of lymphangitis includes conditions such as contact dermatitis, cellulitis, thrombophlebitis, fasciitis, and myositis. The incidence, prevalence, and demographic characteristics of lymphangitis are not well-documented. Common risk factors for developing lymphangitis include trauma, chronic disorders, and skin infections. The natural history, complications, prognosis, clinical presentation, and physical findings of lymphangitis vary widely depending on its etiology. Certain non-specific laboratory findings, when present alongside lymphangitis, may suggest underlying causes. Examples of such tests include complete blood count (CBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), and serology titers. The primary treatment for lymphangitis is antimicrobial therapy. Supportive measures include the use of analgesics, anti-inflammatory agents, and warm compresses. In cases of nodular lymphangitis complicated by abscess formation and lymphedema, surgical intervention may be necessary in addition to appropriate medical therapy. There is no established primary prevention strategy for lymphangitis. However, secondary prevention involves addressing recurrent skin infections, which are often caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococci. Prophylactic antibiotic administration can reduce the risk of these infections progressing to lymphangitis. Historically, lymphangitis has been recognized as an ancient disease, but its exact origins are not well understood. Specific historical perspectives on individual infections are discussed in detail elsewhere. There is no diagnostic imaging, such as X-rays or CT scans, specifically associated with lymphangitis. Similarly, there are no other diagnostic findings unique to this condition. The clinical presentation of lymphangitis, such as red streaks on the skin, can mimic other conditions like contact dermatitis, cellulitis, thrombophlebitis, fasciitis, and myositis. Key clinical findings that help differentiate lymphangitis include red linear streaks extending proximally from a distal site of infection, tender regional lymphadenopathy, fever, and a history of infection by causative organisms. The epidemiology and demographics of lymphangitis are poorly studied, and specific data for individual infections are discussed separately. Similarly, the history, symptoms, and physical examination findings of lymphangitis depend on its underlying cause and are detailed for specific infections elsewhere. There are no diagnostic laboratory findings unique to lymphangitis. However, non-specific laboratory abnormalities, such as elevated inflammatory markers (e.g., ESR, CRP) or abnormal CBC results, may suggest underlying causes. There are no diagnostic findings on X-rays, CT scans, or other imaging modalities specifically associated with lymphangitis. The cornerstone of treatment for lymphangitis is antimicrobial therapy, tailored to the causative organism. Supportive therapies, including analgesics, anti-inflammatory agents, and warm compresses, are also employed. In cases of recurrent skin infections caused by group A beta-hemolytic streptococci, prophylactic antibiotics can help prevent the progression to lymphangitis.
